task_instruction: Give notes on the pilot's cold open
task_details: Pilot: single-camera, 22-minute sitcom about Mina, a 30-something Korean-American dating app writer in LA. Cold open: Mina at a speed-dating event accidentally uses her boss's promo line and gets swarmed. Provide developmental notes focusing on tone, setup, and punchline clarity. Offer one concrete line swap and staging suggestion.
personalized: Love the cold open energy — it snaps. Mina's voice is sharp and the physical gag of the wrong promo line landing is gold. Cut the first two beats where we linger on other tables; they dilute Mina's moment. Make the camera stay on her reaction longer (builds sympathy and gives us the comic beat). Swap the clunky punchline. Try: "Congratulations, you've just matched with corporate synergy" instead of the current throwaway. That lands the absurdity and keeps the joke on-brand. Stage it so Mina's eyes dart to her boss across the room right after the line (immediately raises stakes). Small trim, bigger reaction, stronger payoff.

task_instruction: Notes on clarifying the A-story setup in Act One
task_details: Pilot A-story: Mina gets tasked to write a viral 'dating advice' column under a pseudonym, which forces her to confront her own singlehood publicly. Act One currently introduces the assignment mid-scene. Provide notes to make the inciting incident clearer and suggest a line that establishes the assignment immediately.
personalized: Nice emotional hook — the premise of writing advice you don't follow is relatable. Right now the assignment revelation is buried; we don't feel Mina's stakes early enough. Move the assignment beat to the opening of Act One. Make the inciting line hit at first beat: "Boss: You're the voice people think they want. Write it. Yesterday." That immediately clarifies the external task (viral column) and forces Mina's internal conflict (do I fake this?). Tighten the scene so Mina has one clear choice before leaving the office (accept publicly or ghost it). That gives every following beat momentum and explains why she keeps making defensive, self-sabotaging jokes.

task_instruction: Offer notes on integrating the B-story more organically
task_details: B-story: Mina's roommate, Jess, is trying to start a plant-sitting side hustle and wants Mina's promotional help. Currently the B-story appears as an afterthought in Act Two and doesn't echo A-story themes. Suggest ways to weave it thematically and provide a short suggested line where Mina ties both stories together.

Add a connecting line when Mina drafts the promo: "If we can sell this as 'plant therapy' we can sell me as 'dating therapy' — same hustle, different angle." (Shows theme: performative expertise.) That link will make jokes land deeper and let the B-story escalate in emotional resonance rather than just comic relief.

task_instruction: Refine the inciting incident's emotional clarity
task_details: Scene: Mina reads negative comments under her predecessor's column and impulsively posts a sarcastic reply which goes viral. Notes should focus on tightening her motivation for replying and suggest a concise internal thought line to justify the action.
personalized: The viral moment is exciting. We need a clearer personal hook for why Mina replies. Right now it feels reactionary rather than motivated. Give her an internal beat — maybe humiliation from a past 'advice fail' (family or ex) that makes her more defensive. Try this internal thought-action: Mina scrolls, winces, then types: "Oh look, the experts again." She posts sarcastically. (Small line, big subtext: she can't resist correcting injustice.) That tiny motivation will make the viral outcome feel earned and keep audience sympathy for her mistake.

task_instruction: Suggest act break placement and runtime fixes
task_details: Pilot running long by five minutes. Specifically, Act Two bleeds into Act Three with a repetitive montage and a long phone-call scene. Provide notes on where to cut and how to tighten transitions to hit a 22-minute runtime, including a suggested cut line.
personalized: Show is running warm. Love the montage but it's currently redundant. Cut the last two beats of the montage and move that emotional beat into the phone call as a micro-flash. Trim the phone call: drop the second 'I'm fine' exchange (it's doing the same work as the first). Make the cut with this direction: "Replace montage beat 'Mina scrolls sadly' with 'Mina answers, 'No, I'm great' (and hangs up).'" That preserves the emotional arc, keeps the momentum, and trims the runtime without losing the laugh or the stake.

task_instruction: Polish the protagonist's voice to be more distinct
task_details: Feedback needed on Mina's dialogue in the pilot. Currently she's witty but sometimes generic. Provide notes to sharpen her voice, include specific phrasing swaps, and incorporate one Korean-language throwaway that fits her character without being forced.

And in the family scene, add a casual Korean throwaway: Have her mutter, 'Eomma would roast me for this' (small, authentic, not explanatory). That anchors her culturally and makes her phrasing unique. Keep the punchlines fast; let the quieter, culturally specific beats land between the jokes.

task_instruction: Check cultural authenticity for family scenes
task_details: Family scene at a Korean family dinner: Mina returns home after viral mishap. Concerns: dialogue feels stereotyped and explanatory. Provide notes to make interactions authentic, recommend one natural Korean word/gesture, and suggest cutting an explanatory line.

Remove the explanatory beat 'You know how we do kimchi' and replace it with a lived detail. Have Eomma slide a plate across the table and say, 'Eat before you complain' (practical love). Add a small gesture: Eomma tucking the edge of Mina's napkin under her chin without comment. And a single, organic Korean line — 'Jal meokkesseumnida' as Mina says grace under her breath — signals cultural authenticity without exposition. Let actions speak; the audience will fill in the rest.

task_instruction: Tighten joke density and punchline placement

In the whiteboard scene, move the small gag about 'dating metrics' to later and replace it with a stronger, character-driven punch: "We're optimizing human heartbreak for engagement" as the line for Eric. Rhythm matters; a well-placed quiet line will land harder than three medium ones in a row.

task_instruction: Adjust physical comedy beats for clarity
task_details: Scene: Mina has a pratfall at a launch party that currently reads messy on page. Notes should make the physical gag clear, safe, and funny while trimming excess description. Provide a suggested stage direction and a punchline to follow the fall.
personalized: Physical comedy is great when it's concise. Right now the fall has too many setup paragraphs. Tighten to the essentials: describe the build (wine glass, slick tile), the misstep, the reaction. Simplify stage direction: 'Mina slips. Glass arcs. She turns it into a juggling bit to save face.' After the fall, give her a defensive punchline to save dignity: "You saw nothing. That was performance art." (This keeps her smart and salvage-oriented.) Make sure choreography is practical for production and that the joke comes from defense, not humiliation.

task_instruction: Tighten the pilot's tag for emotional payoff

task_instruction: Draft a concise table-read feedback email summary

Example swap for the bodega pause: replace 'I can't believe you like that' with 'You too? I thought I was the only late-night tragic.' That tiny beat gave the actors room to breathe and the laugh. Overall: strong, just needs rhythmic tightening.

These changes make the pilot easier to pitch: clearer premise, cohesive theme, and a hook the network can market.

task_details: Pilot's tone wavers between single-camera intimacy and multi-camera punchline cadence. Provide notes to commit to a tone and suggest how to stage one scene to reflect that choice, including a sample line delivery note.

In the bodega scene, favor quiet beats and cutaway images instead of line-by-line bang-bangs. Direction note: deliver Mina's punchline as a quiet, deadpan aside, not a wave-to-the-audience joke. Use the line, 'I'll take the one with more baggage' delivered under her breath as she reaches for the snack (camera lingers). That keeps tone consistent and lets small comedy feel sharp rather than shouty.

persona.name: Marko Petrović
persona.demographics: Belgrade, Serbia; Serbian; raised in a small village near Niš, has lived and worked across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Croatia
persona.profession: Senior GIS Analyst & Cartographer — Village-scale mapping and spatial data analyst
persona.education: MSc in Geomatics (University of Belgrade); BSc in Geography; Esri ArcGIS Professional Certification; Certified QGIS trainer; UAV/drone mapping course
persona.brief_background: Marko blends time in the field with long evenings at his workstation, stitching together satellite imagery, drone captures and interviews with elders to produce detailed village maps. He submits edits to OpenStreetMap, trains local volunteers to collect GPS points and writes small scripts to automate data cleaning. He looks for patterns in settlement changes and infrastructure gaps so NGOs and municipal planners can make practical decisions.
persona.interests_lifestyle: drone piloting and aerial photography, OpenStreetMap contributions, hiking and field surveys in rural areas, Balkan folk music and village festivals, Python and R scripting for spatial analysis, map design and cartographic aesthetics, weekend camping with a field GPS, mentoring university students

general_writing_style.tone: Professional and pragmatic with a quietly warm, mentoring undercurrent. Prefers clear, actionable communication — answers questions directly, flags uncertainties, and defers to local knowledge when relevant. Slightly informal with colleagues and volunteers, more formal with institutional partners or written deliverables.
general_writing_style.syntax: Predominantly short to medium-length declarative and imperative sentences for instructions and reports, with occasional longer complex sentences when explaining methodology or interpreting spatial patterns. Often structures technical notes as stepwise numbered instructions or compact paragraphs with parenthetical clarifications (e.g., coordinates, CRS codes). Rarely uses ornate language; prioritizes clarity and reproducibility.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Mixes GIS and cartographic terminology with local place-language; routinely uses terms like "DEM", "orthorectify", "NDVI", "shapefile", "raster/vector", "GPX" and CRS tags such as "EPSG:4326". Uses metric units (meters, hectares, kilometres) and local toponyms with diacritics (e.g., "selo", "Niš", "Belgrade") when referring to field sites. Prefers domain-specific verbs like "georeference", "reproject", "tile", "clip", "attribute" and practical phrases such as "field survey" and "push edits to OSM."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequently opens notes with pragmatic markers like "Quick note:", "FYI," or "Tip:" and closes offers to help with "If you want, I can…" or "Let me know and I’ll…". Uses contractions in informal exchanges ("I'll", "can't", "we've") and includes inline technical reminders such as "check projection", "reproject to EPSG:3857" or "push to OSM"; also habitually appends coordinates or examples in parentheses, e.g., "(43.3155 N, 21.8958 E)".

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: Email to a municipal planner about a submitted village map and recommended infrastructure priorities.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Concise, formal-professional with clear action items and measurable recommendations. Use short declarative sentences for each recommendation, include metric units and references to specific map layers, and close with an offer to provide technical files or a short walkthrough.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Use pragmatic openers like "Quick note:" and direct requests such as "Please review the attached shapefile." Include domain tags and units in-line: "reproject to EPSG:4326", "buffer 50 m", "area: 2.4 ha". Typical phrases: "Please confirm", "I recommend", "If you want, I can provide...". Use numbered instruction language in prose: "First, check the road layer; then clip to the municipal boundary."

task_instruction: Request review of submitted village map and recommend road repair priorities.
task_details: Send an email to the municipal planner about a completed village map for selo Donja Reka. Highlight three road segments needing urgent repair based on road layer and DEM slope analysis. Include lengths in metres, reference layers (roads, DEM, landuse), suggest a 50 m buffer for drainage, and request confirmation. Offer technical files and walkthrough.
personalized: Quick note: I uploaded the village map for selo Donja Reka to the project folder and pushed the road edits to the roads layer. Please review the attached shapefile. Based on the road layer and the DEM (1 m UAV DEM, reproject to EPSG:4326) I recommend prioritising three segments. First, the east–west connector near the creek needs immediate resurfacing; length: 820 m; slope >10% at the north approach. Second, the main access to the school requires concrete reinforcement; length: 460 m; adjacent landuse: agricultural, prone to rutting after rain. Third, the hillside lane to selo Gornji Potok needs retaining at two points; length: 160 m; buffer 50 m recommended for drainage work. Please confirm which segment you want budgeted this quarter. I can provide the shapefile (roads_repair_DonjaReka.shp), the DEM (tiff, EPSG:3857) and a short walkthrough of the layers if you want. Let me know and I’ll schedule a 20‑minute call.

task_instruction: Propose increasing ground sample points per village after field trials.
task_details: Explain that initial field test used 3 sample points per selo and showed high local variance. Recommend increasing to 6 sample points per selo, describe how to select points (spread across settlement extents), mention GPS averaging and time per point, and invite manager input.
personalized: FYI, quick note from the field tests in selo Donji Brijeg (43.2001 N, 21.6543 E). The three sample points we collected per selo missed intra-settlement variability for building condition and access paths. If we increase sample points to 6 per selo and space them across the settlement footprint, we should capture the variance without doubling field time. Use GPX waypoints for each position, allow a 10 second averaging at each waypoint to improve accuracy, and tag each point with the same attribute schema we used in the pilot (owner_type, structure_material, condition_score). This will cost about 20% more field time but reduce classification uncertainty when we aggregate to selo level. If you want, I can model the added time per cluster and update the schedule. Let me know and I'll update the protocol.

If we switch to the standardized schema now, we can push the updated form to all devices and reduce cleaning time by at least one day per municipality. I can prepare the KoBo export and a short training note for volunteers. Let me know and I'll update the protocol.

task_instruction: Suggest changing GPS collection settings to improve accuracy.
task_details: Field GPS units were in single-shot mode. Recommend enabling WAAS/EGNOS where available, using 10-second averaging, record HDOP, and ask to log GPS device model. Explain expected accuracy improvement and impact on time.
personalized: FYI, I checked the raw GPX from last week and many fixes are single-shot with variable HDOP. If we enable WAAS/EGNOS on tablets where available and require a 10-second averaging for waypoint capture, we could reduce horizontal error from ~6–8 m to ~2–3 m in open areas. Please also ask teams to record the GPS device model in the collector_id field so we can compare performance. The averaging adds about 10 seconds per point but will cut attribute-location mismatches during matching to building footprints. If you want, I can draft the short SOP for GPS settings. Let me know and I'll update the protocol.

task_instruction: Propose drone flight parameter changes for orthophoto consistency.
task_details: After drone flights over selo Gornje, imagery overlap was inconsistent. Recommend flight altitude 120 m AGL, frontlap 80%, sidelap 75%, capture in RAW, include ground control points, and note orthorectify steps and CRS.
personalized: Quick update: drone strips over selo Gornje showed variable overlap and visible seams after orthorectify. This will slightly increase flight time but reduce manual mosaic correction. I can update the flight SOP and provide the QGIS workflow for orthorectify (GCP tie, bundle block, DSM use). Let me know and I'll update the protocol.

Let me know and I'll update the protocol.

Reproject final outputs to EPSG:3857 for mapping if requested, but log raw coordinates in EPSG:4326. Note any signal obstructions in the field notebook. Safe fieldwork — call me if you see persistent accuracy issues.

task_instruction: Field route and timing plan

Keep one person with the route sheet and confirm cell coverage points before entering valleys. Charge devices before departure and bring printed maps. Safe fieldwork — call me if timing slips or roads are blocked.

task_instruction: Dealing with livestock and guard dogs
task_details: Instruct volunteers on approaching livestock, handling confrontations with dogs, and respect for private property. Include example phrases for consent and an emergency action.
personalized: Quick checklist: Do not approach livestock closely; keep a wide berth and expand your path to avoid herds. If you meet a guard dog, stay calm, avoid eye contact, back away slowly and use a loud, firm voice. If property access is needed, ask the resident for permission, state purpose clearly, and note consent with name and time (e.g., Marko, 09:15). If threatened, retreat to a vehicle or group and call the team lead. Log any aggressive encounters with coordinates for the record (43.305 N, 21.900 E). Safe fieldwork — call me if a situation escalates.

task_instruction: Data backup and upload procedure

task_instruction: OSM tagging and edit guidelines

task_instruction: Consent and community interaction script
task_details: Provide volunteers with concise phrasing for requesting consent to survey on private land, greeting templates, and recordkeeping requirements. Include example phrases and contact offer.
personalized: Reminder: Greet people politely and introduce yourself and the project purpose before entering private land. Use simple phrasing: "We are mapping local infrastructure for municipal planning; may we take a few GPS points on your property?" Note the person's name, time, and consent status in the log. Offer the leaflet and a phone number for follow-up. Respect refusals and move on without dispute. If unsure, defer to the local coordinator. Safe fieldwork — call me if you need help getting permission.

task_instruction: Mapping water features and flood-prone areas
task_details: Instructions for surveying streams, wells, and flooded areas: sample points, photo angles, safety near water, and logging seasonal information. Include example coordinates and data attributes to capture.
personalized: Quick checklist: Record water points with coordinates (EPSG:4326), water source type, and condition (dry/seasonal/permanent). Take upstream and downstream photos and one close-up of source structure. Avoid working on slick banks and use a pole if collecting samples. Note recent flood marks and approximate height above ground in metres. Flag channels needing further hydrological assessment for the team. Safe fieldwork — call me if you encounter unsafe water conditions.

task_instruction: Steep terrain and landslide risk warning
task_details: Warn volunteers about working on slopes: approaching ridgelines, footwear, GPS anchoring, and actions if instability observed. Include example coordinates and closure actions.
personalized: Reminder: Avoid working alone on steep slopes and keep at least one person on stable ground when approaching edges. Wear ankle-support boots and use trekking poles. Do not place equipment on loose scree; set GCPs on solid ground. If you see cracks or fresh slides, back away immediately and record location (e.g., 43.300 N, 21.880 E). Notify the team lead for a quick assessment and mark the area on the map. Safe fieldwork — call me if you suspect active instability.

task_instruction: Handling cultural and sensitive sites
task_details: Instruct volunteers on respectful behavior near religious, burial or culturally sensitive sites, what to record and what to avoid. Include example phrasing for asking permission and a contact for cultural questions.
personalized: Quick checklist: Treat cultural and religious sites with respect. Do not enter fenced or clearly sacred areas without explicit permission. Ask elders or caretakers for guidance and record their names and consent. Mark sensitive sites in the field notes and flag them for restricted public sharing. Safe fieldwork — call me if you need to verify cultural protocols.

task_instruction: Vehicle and road safety guidance
task_details: Advise volunteers on driving on rural roads, parking near survey sites, loading equipment, and what to do if the vehicle gets stuck. Include example checkpoint coordinates and emergency contact instruction.
personalized: Reminder: Drive slowly on unpaved roads and avoid steep muddy tracks after rain. Park off the carriageway and set hazard lights when stopping. Load equipment carefully to avoid shifting; tie drone cases and GPS boxes securely. If a vehicle gets stuck, stay with it, call for towing and provide coordinates (e.g., 43.325 N, 21.910 E). Keep a shovel and tow rope in each vehicle. Safe fieldwork — call me if vehicles are immobilized.

task_instruction: Interviewing elders and qualitative notes

Store audio files with filenames linking to the site ID. Safe fieldwork — call me if consent is refused or someone is uncomfortable.

task_instruction: Night survey safety and lighting protocol
task_details: Explain how to conduct safe night surveys: lighting equipment, reflective clothing, GPS logging in low light, and limits on night work. Include example device suggestions and closing support offer.
personalized: Reminder: Only perform night surveys if pre-approved. Use headlamps with red/white modes and carry spare batteries. Wear reflective vests and stay in groups near roads. Limit night work to simple tasks and return to base by agreed curfew. Safe fieldwork — call me if you feel unsafe and we'll pull out the team.

task_instruction: Sample point numbering and attribute protocol

task_instruction: Reporting hazardous findings (chemical/biological)
task_details: Tell volunteers how to identify and report hazardous sites such as waste dumps, chemical spills, or sick livestock. Include safety distance, photo policy, logging, and who to inform.
personalized: Reminder: Do not approach obvious hazardous waste or sick animals. Stay at least 30 m away and photograph from a safe distance, noting wind direction and visible signs. Record coordinates (EPSG:4326), time, and a short description. Mark the site as 'HAZARD' in the log and notify the team lead immediately. Avoid contact and do not disturb any containers. If exposure occurs, wash with soap and seek medical help. Safe fieldwork — call me immediately for any hazardous encounters.

task_instruction: Mapping utilities and powerline safety
task_details: Provide instructions for mapping electrical infrastructure safely: safe distances, photographing poles, tagging attributes, and what to avoid. Include example coordinate and closure.
personalized: Quick checklist: Maintain a safe distance from powerlines and substations; do not climb poles or touch exposed wires. Photograph poles from the ground and record pole ID, line type, and apparent condition. Note underground cable markers and access points but do not excavate or open cabinets. Record coordinates (e.g., 43.308 N, 21.898 E) and tag utility features for follow-up. Safe fieldwork — call me if you find damaged infrastructure and we'll notify the utility company.

task_instruction: Training and mentoring new volunteers in the field
task_details: Provide an email guiding experienced volunteers to mentor new recruits: shadowing, demonstration tasks, gradual independence, and feedback. Include coordinate examples and offer to assist with training materials.
personalized: Quick checklist: Pair each new volunteer with an experienced mapper for the first two days. Demonstrate one full point collection from approach to upload and then let the novice repeat under supervision. Review their first ten points for accuracy and discuss errors on the spot. Encourage questions and give positive feedback. Keep the training area simple (example sector near 43.312 N, 21.893 E). If you want, I can join the first session or prepare a quick cheat-sheet. Safe fieldwork — call me if training needs extra time.

task_instruction: Contingency for illness or COVID symptoms
task_details: Advise volunteers on steps if they develop symptoms: isolating, notifying team, returning to base, data handover, and follow-up. Include example symptom checklist and contact process.
personalized: Reminder: If you develop fever, cough, or other COVID-like symptoms, stop fieldwork and isolate immediately. Inform the team lead and return to base with mask on or arrange pickup. Do not return to the field until cleared. Safe fieldwork — call me and I'll coordinate replacements and reporting.

task_instruction: Mapping trails and pedestrian paths
task_details: Give volunteers instructions specific to mapping informal trails: how to trace, record width/surface, and capture erosion features. Include example coordinate and upload timeframe.
personalized: Quick checklist: Trace trails by walking their centerline and record surface type and approximate width in metres. Photograph sections showing erosion, steps, or markers. Upload trail edits within 48 hours and flag any newly built or blocked paths. Safe fieldwork — call me if you find a trail that requires urgent maintenance.

task_instruction: Handling sensitive personal data and privacy
task_details: Explain how to treat personal data collected during surveys: consent, anonymization, storage and sharing rules. Include example of redaction and whom to contact for guidance.

task_instruction: End-of-day checklist before leaving the field
task_details: Provide volunteers with a concise end-of-day routine: file backups, device shutdown, battery charging, equipment check, and handover notes for the next day. Include example filenames and sign-off.
personalized: Quick checklist: Backup all data to external drive and cloud (villageID_YYYYMMDD). Verify all photos and GPS logs are included. Switch off devices only after successful backups. Charge batteries overnight and label them for tomorrow. Pack out all trash and secure equipment in locked vehicles. Leave a short handover note with outstanding tasks and coordinates for next start (e.g., resume at 43.318 N, 21.896 E). Safe fieldwork — call me if anything is missing at handover.

Sources were GPS traces from July 2025 and field notes; imagery used for alignment was orthophoto 2024-09-03. If you'd prefer different tagging or want me to revert any of these, say so and I'll roll it back.

task_instruction: Propose tagging guideline for local churches and denominations
task_details: Propose a small tagging convention: include denomination, name:sr, and historical name in alt_name. Provide example tag snippets and invite community discussion and acceptance.

I used that pattern in changeset #12346278 for three local churches. If you prefer a different scheme or want me to change existing tags, discuss here and I’ll adjust.

task_instruction: Ask for clarification on chosen projection and CRS settings.
task_details: Student submitted a QGIS project and a PDF map for a village mapping assignment. The project includes a drone orthomosaic (GeoTIFF), a DEM (GeoTIFF), and vector layers (roads.shp, buildings.shp). The instructor wants clarification on which CRS was used, why, and whether it matches municipality standards. Request the student to confirm CRS for each layer, explain choice, and provide steps to reproject if needed.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. I can see the orthomosaic and building footprints, but the CRS isn't clear in the PDF. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 if your final deliverable is web-tiling or EPSG:3857-based basemaps; otherwise reproject to the local projected CRS used by the municipality (give EPSG code). Quick note: check projection on each layer in QGIS (right-click layer > Properties > Source). Also check nodata values on the orthomosaic and DEM so seamless mosaics don't show artifacts. Avoid overlapping labels on the main street names — reduce font size or use data-defined placement. If you want, I can review the QGIS project file and confirm the correct CRS settings and show exact reprojection steps (reproject raster via Warp (GDAL), vectors via Reproject layer). Let me know and I’ll guide you through the reproject workflow and produce a short checklist for submission.

task_instruction: Provide constructive feedback on symbology choices and color ramps.
task_details: Student used default color ramps for land use categories and a single hillshade layer. The assignment asks for clear differentiation between agricultural, forest, built-up, and water areas and a readable hillshade for relief. Offer feedback on color contrast, hillshade blend modes, and accessible palettes. Suggest concrete palette names and QGIS settings.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Your land-use categories are present, but the default color ramp makes agricultural and forest areas hard to distinguish. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 if you plan to overlay web tiles, but for print maps a local metric CRS is often better. Quick tip: use a qualitative palette such as ColorBrewer's 'Set2' for land-use polygons and a semi-transparent neutral brown for hillshade set to Multiply blend at 30–40% opacity. Also check nodata values on the classified raster so transparent areas don't render as white patches. Avoid overlapping labels by switching to 'Around point' placement or using smaller fonts for secondary features. If you want, I can review the QGIS project file and suggest exact color hex codes and layer-order settings to improve legibility.

task_instruction: Request clarification about GPS field data collection and coordinate accuracy.
task_details: Student attached a GPX track and several GPX waypoints collected during a field survey. The assignment requires accuracy estimates and metadata (device model, datum, time). Ask for device details, estimated horizontal accuracy, and whether post-processing was done. Suggest how to document and possibly improve accuracy.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The GPX waypoints look useful, but I need more on accuracy. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 for web display only; keep raw GPX in EPSG:4326 and record datum and device settings. Please tell me the GPS device model, approximate horizontal accuracy reported (e.g., 3–8 m), and whether you used differential correction or SBAS. Check nodata values are not relevant to GPX but make sure timestamps are correct and timezone-consistent. Avoid overlapping labels in the final map by clustering waypoint labels or using numbered callouts with a table. If you want, I can review the GPX in QGIS, estimate positional errors relative to known control points, and suggest post-processing steps.

task_instruction: Advise on handling no-data and mosaic seams in drone orthomosaic.
task_details: Student's orthomosaic shows seam lines and black edges where no-data exists; DEM has holes. Ask for original imagery metadata, processing method, and request reprocessing tips. Provide step-by-step guidance on handling no-data, feathering, and filling DEM holes, and mention tools (GDAL/gdalwarp, QGIS Raster > Align Rasters).
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The orthomosaic seams and black edges indicate no-data issues from the mosaic process. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only when preparing web outputs; for processing keep the native projection. First, check nodata values in the GeoTIFF (gdalinfo). Use gdalwarp to set an explicit -dstnodata and to align pixels if needed. For the DEM, run a small focal fill to interpolate shallow holes or use the 'Fill nodata' GDAL tool with a small maximum distance. Avoid overlapping labels near seam areas by moving label anchors away from boundaries. If you want, I can review the orthomosaic metadata and run a quick gdalwarp command to produce a cleaned version and show the exact commands.

task_instruction: Comment on labeling strategy and readability on the submitted map.
task_details: Student placed many labels directly on small polygons and roads resulting in clutter. The assignment requires readable labels at 1:10,000 scale. Provide suggestions for label priority, font sizes, buffer settings, and data-defined placement to reduce overlaps.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The label clutter reduces readability at 1:10,000. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web previews; for scale-based labeling set the project CRS to a local metric CRS so label distances are accurate. Prioritize primary features (village name, major roads) and use smaller fonts with halo buffers for secondary features. In QGIS, enable 'Avoid overlap' and use data-defined placement to shift labels along roads. Also check nodata values in background rasters so transparent areas don't interfere with labels. Avoid overlapping labels by setting scale-based visibility and using callouts for dense clusters. If you want, I can open your QGIS project, tweak the labeling rules, and send a before/after PDF.

task_instruction: Give guidance on exporting map for print and digital submission.
task_details: Student asks how to export a high-resolution PDF and a web-friendly PNG. Provide recommended DPI for print, color mode, embedding fonts, and steps to create web tiles or a compressed PNG. Mention file sizes and naming conventions.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. For print submit a 300 DPI PDF with CMYK if the printer requires it; otherwise 300 DPI RGB is fine for academic submission. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web tile generation; keep the print export in your project CRS to avoid reprojection resampling. Check nodata values so transparent zones render correctly in export. Avoid overlapping labels by exporting with 'Simplify geometries' off and review at full scale before finalizing. For web, export a 1500–2000 px PNG and consider creating slippy tiles (XYZ) at zoom levels 15–17. If you want, I can open your project and export both a print-ready PDF and a web-optimized PNG with recommended settings and filenames.

task_instruction: Suggest improvements to attribute data and schema for buildings layer.
task_details: Student's buildings.shp has name and type fields but inconsistent attribute values and missing construction years. Recommend schema changes, controlled vocabularies, and methods to clean attributes using Python or QGIS Field Calculator. Offer to help write cleaning scripts.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The buildings attribute table needs cleaning. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web outputs; keep attribute edits CRS-agnostic. Create a controlled vocabulary for 'type' (residential, commercial, agricultural) and standardize strings with lower-case and no diacritics only if instructed; otherwise preserve local toponyms like 'selo' and 'kuća'. Use QGIS Field Calculator to normalize values and a short Python script (pandas or geopandas) for batch fixes. Also check nodata values in attribute exports (NULLs) and record them in metadata. Avoid overlapping labels on building names by limiting labels to significant features. If you want, I can draft a small geopandas script to clean the table and run it on your shapefile.

task_instruction: Review methodology for creating contours from DEM.
task_details: Student derived 1 m contours from a 5 m DEM and included them on the map. Explain issues with contour interval vs DEM resolution, smoothing, and labeling contour lines. Ask for DEM source and recommend proper contour intervals and settings.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Generating 1 m contours from a 5 m DEM creates artificial precision. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for visualization; for contour generation keep the DEM in its native projected CRS so vertical distance matches units. Use contour intervals that match DEM resolution — 5 or 10 m would be appropriate for a 5 m DEM. Apply slight smoothing to avoid noisy lines and label every fifth contour for readability. Check nodata values in the DEM so contours don't trace around holes. Avoid overlapping labels with contour labels by using automated label placement and buffer. If you want, I can look at your DEM (send source and EPSG) and suggest the optimal contour interval and smoothing settings.

task_instruction: Provide feedback on the legend and map annotation choices.
task_details: Student's legend contains too many items and small symbols. The assignment requires a clear, compact legend and north arrow and scale bar. Suggest reordering, grouping symbols, and concise legend text.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The legend is overloaded and hard to read at a glance. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web use; legend design is independent of CRS. Group similar features (roads: primary/secondary/local) and use concise labels like 'Road (local)'. Reduce symbol count by aggregating minor classes into 'Other'. Check nodata values so legend doesn't unintentionally include nodata as a category. Avoid overlapping labels by spacing legend entries and using leader lines where necessary. If you want, I can edit your legend layout in the print composer and return a compact version with recommended font sizes and ordering.

task_instruction: Ask about ethical and privacy considerations for publishing building-level data.
task_details: Student mapped private houses with ownership notes and plans to publish online. Request that they anonymize sensitive attributes, explain consent procedures used in field surveys, and suggest best practices for publishing sensitive spatial data.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Publishing building-level data with ownership notes raises privacy concerns. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for map tiles; privacy decisions are independent of CRS. Remove or anonymize personally identifiable information and generalize building footprints if necessary (buffer by a few meters or aggregate to block-level). Document consent obtained during field surveys and record which features were collected with explicit permission. Also check nodata values in exported datasets and ensure you don't accidentally publish empty attribute fields containing sensitive information. Avoid overlapping labels that reveal private details. If you want, I can review your attribute table for sensitive fields and suggest anonymization options before you publish or push edits to OSM.

task_instruction: Recommend steps to improve automated classification accuracy (land cover).
task_details: Student performed supervised classification of Sentinel-2 imagery but reports misclassification between crops and grassland. Ask for training sample sizes, classifier used, and suggest augmentations like NDVI, texture measures, and post-class filtering. Offer a quick validation protocol.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Misclassification between crops and grassland is common with only spectral bands. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web mapping; keep analysis in a projected CRS like UTM for accurate area calculations. Add NDVI and seasonal indices, include texture measures (GLCM) and increase training samples per class across spatial variability. Check nodata values in Sentinel-2 scenes and mask clouds before classification. Apply a majority filter post-classification to remove salt-and-pepper noise. Avoid overlapping labels by creating a simplified land-cover legend. If you want, I can review your training samples and run a cross-validation routine to estimate accuracy and suggest improvements.

task_instruction: Offer help debugging a Python script used to clean attribute data.
task_details: Student attached a short Python script using geopandas to standardize building types but it throws a KeyError. Ask for the dataset and provide debugging suggestions and a corrected script snippet. Offer to run the script and return results.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The KeyError likely means the field name used in the script doesn't match the shapefile attribute. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only when creating web-derived outputs; the script should work on geometries regardless of CRS but field names must match. Open the shapefile in QGIS, copy the exact column name (watch for trailing spaces or uppercase), and update your script accordingly. Also check nodata-equivalent NULLs in the attribute table which can cause logic errors. Avoid overlapping labels by ensuring the geometry cleanup step doesn't create duplicate features. If you want, I can run your script, fix the field reference, and return a corrected version with comments.

If you want, I can review your planned changeset text and the GPX/imagery alignment before you upload to OSM.

task_instruction: Suggest how to perform and document a spatial accuracy assessment.
task_details: Student claims positional accuracy but did not perform formal assessment. Provide a simple protocol using ground control points, RMSE calculation, and suggested sample sizes. Ask for available GCPs and offer to run the assessment.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Claims of positional accuracy need a formal check. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for display; perform accuracy assessment in a local projected CRS (meters). Collect at least 10 well-distributed ground control points (GCPs) measured with a survey-grade or high-accuracy GNSS and calculate RMSE. Use QGIS 'Vector > Analysis Tools > Distance to nearest hub' or a short Python script to compute errors and summarize them. Check nodata values so points near DEM holes are excluded. Avoid overlapping labels in accuracy tables by presenting results in a simple table. If you want, I can calculate RMSE from your GCPs and produce a short methods paragraph for your report.

Increase font sizes for main labels, reduce symbology for minor categories, and use inset maps for context. Check nodata values so background fills don't create distractions. Avoid overlapping labels by using leader lines for clustered points. If you want, I can open your composer and rearrange elements for A3 output and produce an export-ready file.

task_instruction: Advise on combining hillshade and color-relief for better terrain representation.
task_details: Student used overlay hillshade at full opacity, obscuring color relief. Explain best practices for blending hillshade with color ramps, gamma adjustments, and use of multi-directional hillshades. Provide QGIS layer blending settings.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. A full-opacity hillshade will overpower your color relief. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web previews; terrain rendering works best in the project CRS with units in meters. Use a soft hillshade (Multiply blend) at 20–40% opacity and reduce contrast/gamma to prevent clipping. Consider combining multi-directional hillshades (sun azimuth 315° and 45°) for balanced shading. Check nodata values in DEM so hillshade doesn't create stripes. Avoid overlapping labels over shaded areas by using label buffers. If you want, I can tweak your hillshade and color-relief settings and send screenshots of before/after.

task_instruction: Provide feedback on map scale bar and distance measurement accuracy.
task_details: Student included a scale bar but used degrees units. Explain the mistake and advise on setting scale bar units to metres, appropriate segment length, and ensuring the project CRS supports accurate linear measurement. Offer to fix it in the project.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. The scale bar in degrees is not appropriate for a village-scale map. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web use; for accurate scale bars use a projected CRS with metres (e.g., local UTM). Set the scale bar segments to round metric values (100 m or 500 m) depending on map extent, and lock the map scale when composing. Check nodata values so the scale bar doesn't overlay transparent patches. Avoid overlapping labels near the scale bar by placing it in a corner with clear background. If you want, I can open your project, set the correct CRS, and add a properly calibrated metric scale bar.

task_instruction: Comment on dataset licensing and citation for imagery used.
task_details: Student used satellite and drone imagery but didn't include licensing info. Ask for image providers and dates, and explain how to cite imagery and respect usage restrictions, including drone-flight consent and municipal rules.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Licensing and citation are required. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for viewing on web basemaps; in the report include original CRS and source. Provide provider names, acquisition dates, and license terms (e.g., Sentinel-2 via Copernicus, CC0; drone imagery: proprietary, restricted). Note any flight permissions for drone data. Check nodata values and mention how you masked areas. Avoid overlapping labels that might imply proprietary claims on imagery. If you want, I can draft a short citation block for each dataset and advise on how to display credits on the map.

task_instruction: Suggest methods to generalize vector data for different zoom levels.
task_details: Student created highly detailed vectors which are cluttered at small scales. Recommend simplification algorithms, topology-preserving generalization, and scale-dependent rendering strategies. Offer to produce generalization examples.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Highly detailed vectors will clutter small-scale views. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web tiles; generalization should be done in a metric CRS. Use topology-preserving simplification (Douglas-Peucker with tolerance related to map scale) and create generalized layers for zoomed-out maps. In QGIS, set scale-dependent visibility for layers and simplify geometries on export. Also check nodata values so generalized polygons don't intersect masked areas. Avoid overlapping labels by hiding minor features at smaller scales. If you want, I can prepare a simplified version of your roads/buildings for zoomed-out maps and provide the exact simplification tolerances I used.

task_instruction: Provide feedback on using hillshade to detect man-made terraces and small features.
task_details: Student claims terraces visible in hillshade but hasn't validated with ground truth. Recommend techniques to enhance terrace visibility (slope, curvature, multi-azimuth hillshade) and ask for photos or GPS points for validation.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Hillshade can reveal terraces, but you need validation. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for mapping; perform analysis in a projected CRS for slope/curvature. Generate slope and curvature rasters and use multi-azimuth hillshades to highlight linear terrace edges. Check nodata values in the DEM so derivative rasters are not skewed. Avoid overlapping labels by marking candidate terraces with numbered labels and providing a validation table. If you want, I can run the slope/curvature analysis on your DEM and compare candidate terraces to any field photos or GPS points you can provide.

task_instruction: Request clarification on why the student chose certain symbology for accessibility.
task_details: Student used red/green color scheme that may not be colorblind-friendly. Ask why those choices were made and recommend accessible alternatives and testing methods (simulate colorblindness, use patterns). Offer to test and adjust symbology.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. A red/green scheme can be problematic for colorblind readers. Test symbology with a colorblindness simulator and verify contrast ratios. Also check nodata values so patterns don't overlap transparent regions. Avoid overlapping labels that compound accessibility issues. If you want, I can run a quick accessibility check on your QGIS symbology and propose alternative palettes.

task_instruction: Offer to perform a quick QA/QC check for topology and geometry errors.
task_details: Student is concerned about topology errors (slivers, overlaps, gaps) in vector layers. Offer a QA/QC checklist and describe how to run topological checks in QGIS, repair geometries, and validate polygons. Offer to run fixes if the student provides the files.
personalized: Nice start — good map composition. Topology errors are common and easy to check. You should reproject the raster to EPSG:3857 only for web display; topological checks are best done in a projected CRS where distances are meters. Run QGIS 'Check Geometry Validity' and 'Vector > Geometry Tools > Check validity' to list issues. Use 'Fix Geometries' or topology editing to dissolve slivers and correct overlaps. task_instruction: Propose a 90-minute hands-on workshop on orthophoto production from drone imagery.
task_details: Write an email to a conference organizer proposing a 90-minute hands-on workshop that covers the full orthophoto workflow for village-scale mapping using SfM. Specify learning outcomes as numbered inline items, required equipment (projector, stable Wi‑Fi, 1 laptop with QGIS and OpenDroneMap installed, sample dataset), maximum participants (20), and closing availability for a specific week. Mention CRS and a small local example (coordinates).
personalized:
Dear Conference Organiser,

Proposal: 90-min workshop on orthophoto workflow (SfM) for village-scale mapping. Short lecture followed by a step-by-step hands-on run of a drone dataset, focused on reproducible results for NGOs and local volunteers.

Learning outcomes: 1) set up a SfM project and check projection (EPSG:4326 to EPSG:3857), 2) preprocess and align images (tie points, GCPs), 3) generate orthophoto and DSM and export for OSM. The workshop uses a small dataset from a selo near Niš (approx. 43.3120 N, 21.8950 E) so participants see real village patterns and building footprints.

Requirements: projector, stable Wi‑Fi, power strip, table for 20 people, 1 laptop with QGIS and OpenDroneMap installed (I can provide an Ubuntu VM image), sample dataset (I will send 1 week before). Recommended max participants: 20 to keep it hands-on.

I charge no fee for community-focused conferences; travel costs negotiable. I’m available the week of 16 March 2026 — please confirm and I’ll reserve the dataset and a short pre-workshop checklist.

If you want, I can also run a 30-minute demo lecture instead of hands-on for larger rooms. Looking forward to your reply.

Best regards,
Marko Petrović
Senior GIS Analyst & Cartographer
Belgrade, Serbia

Dear Conference Organiser,

Proposal: 45-min talk on integrating drone orthophotos into OpenStreetMap editing and local mapping projects. The talk is practical and aimed at volunteer mappers, NGO staff and municipal planners.

Learning outcomes: 1) prepare and georeference orthophotos for tracing, 2) streamline attribution and metadata for ethical OSM edits, 3) publish imagery tiles and push edits to OSM safely. I will include quick demos of QGIS and JOSM workflows and a short note on consent and data sensitivity for small communities.

Requirements: projector and stable Wi‑Fi. I will bring a laptop with example tiles and a short handout (PDF) for participants.

I’m available the week of 23 March 2026 — please confirm and I’ll forward the abstract and bio. If you prefer, I can convert this into a 90-min workshop.

Regards,
Marko Petrović
Senior GIS Analyst & Cartographer

Best,
Marko Petrović

Hello,

Proposal: 60-min intermediate workshop on DEM/DTM generation and basic hydrological analysis for village-scale watersheds. The session focuses on turning DSMs from SfM into conditioned DTMs suitable for simple flood/runoff checks.

Learning outcomes: 1) derive DEM and DTM from DSMs and remove vegetation artifacts, 2) run simple hydrological conditioning (sinks, flow accumulation) and interpret results, 3) export results for planners and integrate with OSM layers (buildings, roads). I will use a 1 km2 dataset and demonstrate common pitfalls (terraced fields, orchards).

Requirements: projector, stable Wi‑Fi, 1 laptop with QGIS and SAGA installed, sample DSM/orthophoto (I will provide). Recommended audience: technical planners or GIS-savvy volunteers.

I’m available the week of 13 April 2026 — please confirm and I’ll email the dataset and tool list.

Regards,
Marko

Device: FieldEye Pro v3, SN: FE-PRO-2025-00123
Firmware: v2.1.3
Time: 2026-01-02T08:14:22Z
Location: cerca selo Donji Brežani (43.3201 N, 21.8950 E)

Attached: flightlog_2026-01-02_FEPRO.LOG and a short video (takeoff_attempt_2026-01-02.mp4).
Notes: Barometer and GPS lock were present (GPS: 10 sats, HDOP 0.9). I operate mostly in rural village sites; no strong metal structures nearby. If helpful, I can upload the raw imu.bin from the log.
Please advise next steps.

Quick note: I found a reproducible crash in the Warp (GDAL) tool when reprojecting a small multiband GeoTIFF.
Environment: QGIS 3.16.11, Windows 10 1909, GDAL 3.0.4, CRS source EPSG:4326, target EPSG:3857. Attached: minimal_multiband.tif and repro_case.qgz.

Regards,
Marko Petrović
Belgrade (43.8563 N, 18.4131 E)

personalized:
FYI: Labels move to incorrect locations when changing the project CRS.

Marko Petrović

task_details: A third-party orthophoto import plugin crashes QGIS when loading a 200 MB orthomosaic TIFF on macOS. Provide environment, steps, minimal example file, stacktrace, expected vs actual, and ask for workaround or patch timeline.
personalized:
Quick note: Third-party 'Drone Ortho Import' plugin causes QGIS to crash on macOS when loading an orthomosaic TIFF.

Steps to reproduce: install plugin v1.4.2 > restart QGIS > Plugin > Drone Ortho Import > choose small_ortho_example.tif > click Import.
Observed behaviour: QGIS becomes unresponsive and force quits within 5–10 seconds. No error dialog shown.
stacktrace: Crash log (macOS): Exception Type: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)

  ...
Expected behaviour vs actual behaviour: Plugin should import ortho and add raster layer. Instead QGIS crashes before layer appears.
Notes: Directly opening small_ortho_example.tif via Layer > Add Raster works fine. Problem seems limited to plugin calls into QGIS API.
Please advise whether this should be reported to plugin author or considered an API regression. Request estimated timeline for a fix or suggested plugin workaround.
Regards,
Marko Petrović
Belgrade

Belgrade

Marko Petrović

task_instruction: Report wrong DEM hillshade azimuth rendering after reproject
task_details: DEM hillshade produced by Raster > Hillshade changes apparent illumination direction after reprojecting DEM from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:3857 on Windows. Include steps, environment, sample DEM, stacktrace, expected vs actual, and timeline request.
personalized:
FYI: Hillshade azimuth appears inverted after reprojecting DEM.
Environment: QGIS 3.12.9, Windows 10, original DEM EPSG:4326 (degrees), target EPSG:3857 (meters). Attached: dem_deg.tif and hillshade_repro.qgz.
Steps to reproduce: open hillshade_repro.qgz > add dem_deg.tif > Raster > Projections > Warp (reproject) to EPSG:3857 > Raster > Analysis > Hillshade on reprojected DEM (Z factor 1, azimuth 315, altitude 45).
Observed behaviour: Hillshade appears lit from the opposite direction (azimuth behaves as 135 instead of 315), creating misleading shadows.
stacktrace: QgisMessageLog: 2025-08-22T16:30:05Z "Hillshade: unexpected slope computation: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in arctan2"
Expected behaviour vs actual behaviour: Hillshade azimuth should match specified azimuth and produce consistent illumination. Actual: azimuth reversed after reprojection.
Notes: Performing hillshade before reprojection and then reprojecting the hillshade raster yields correct appearance, but processing pipeline should allow hillshade on reprojected DEM.
Please confirm and provide estimated timeline for a fix or recommended processing order.
Regards,
Marko Petrović
(43.3 N, 21.9 E)

task_instruction: Report symbology crash when using SVG markers with rotation

personalized:
Quick note: SVG marker with data-defined rotation crashes renderer on large layers.
Environment: QGIS 3.4.7, Ubuntu 18.04, SVG marker file used from local svg folder. Attached: points_rotation.shp and svg_rotation.qgz.
Steps to reproduce: open svg_rotation.qgz > style points_layer > Symbol layer type: SVG marker > select svg 'marker.svg' > set rotation to field 'heading' (data-defined) > Apply.
Observed behaviour: QGIS becomes unresponsive during render and shows 'Rendering aborted' then crashes after a few seconds.

Regards,
Marko Petrović

Marko Petrović

task_instruction: Report print composer scale bar rendering wrong scale after project reproject
task_details: Scale bar in Print Layout shows incorrect ground distance after changing project CRS to projected CRS on Windows. Include environment, steps, sample project, stacktrace, expected vs actual, and request timeline.
personalized:
Quick note: Print Layout scale bar shows incorrect ground distances after reprojecting project CRS.
Environment: QGIS 3.8.0, Windows 10, project initially EPSG:4326 then changed to EPSG:32634. Attached: scalebar_bug.qgz.
Steps to reproduce: open scalebar_bug.qgz > Project CRS EPSG:4326 > open Layout 'Main' > note scale bar reading for map at 1:5000 > change Project CRS to EPSG:32634 > refresh Layout.
Observed behaviour: Scale bar now reads 1:10000 while map scale remains 1:5000; measured distances on map disagree with scale bar labels.
stacktrace: QgisMessageLog: 2025-05-02T09:30:12Z "Composer: ScaleBar::updateUnits: Projection conversion error: 'Cannot compute ground distance'
Expected behaviour vs actual behaviour: Scale bar should update and represent accurate ground distances after project CRS change. Actual: labels and units wrong.
Workaround: Manually set scale in layout to match, but this is not reliable for templates.
Please advise and provide an estimated timeline for a fix or a documented procedure to ensure correct scale bar behaviour after reprojection.
Regards,
Marko Petrović

task_instruction: Report 'Select by expression' ignoring CRS when measuring distance function
task_details: Select by expression using distance function returns wrong results when project CRS differs from layer CRS on Linux. Include environment, precise expression used, steps, sample layers, stacktrace, expected vs actual, and timeline request.
personalized:
Quick note: 'select by expression' distance() ignores CRS leading to incorrect selections.
Environment: QGIS 3.20.0, Ubuntu 20.04, layer 'houses' EPSG:4326, project CRS EPSG:3857. Attached: houses.shp, center_point.geojson, select_repro.qgz.
Steps to reproduce: open select_repro.qgz > Vector > Select by Expression > expression: distance($geometry, geom_from_wkt('POINT(21.8958 43.3155)')) < 500 > Run.
Observed behaviour: Features selected are not within 500 metres in ground distance; selected set corresponds to 500 degrees or unprojected units.
stacktrace: QgisMessageLog: 2025-01-20T14:20:11Z "ExpressionContext: distance() computed in layer CRS units rather than project CRS: Warning: unit mismatch"
Expected behaviour vs actual behaviour: distance() should compute geodesic or projected distances respecting desired units. Actual: uses native layer units without conversion.
Workaround: Manually reproject geometries within expression: distance(transform($geometry,'EPSG:4326','EPSG:3857'), ...) works but is verbose.
Please confirm and provide estimated timeline for addressing unit handling in distance().
Regards,
Marko Petrović

personalized:

contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Use outcome language: "Result: 12 villages mapped; 80% coverage of waterpoints." State request directly: "Request: €X for field equipment (GPS + batteries)". Use plain explanations for jargon: "orthophoto (stitched aerial imagery)" and close: "Can we schedule a 30‑min call?"

task_instruction: Request funds to scale a successful village mapping model to a neighboring municipality.
task_details: Write an email summarising the model's success (measurable indicators from initial municipality), outline the scale plan and expected outputs for the neighbouring municipality, request a clear budget for scaling, and end with a 30-minute call offer.
personalized:
Dear [Name],

Result: Our village mapping model in Municipality A produced verified datasets for 46 villages, informed three municipal investment decisions and trained 40 volunteers. The model is ready to be adapted for neighbouring Municipality B.

Request: €27,500 to scale the model to Municipality B (field teams, training, community outreach, data processing and delivery). Expected outputs: full mapping coverage of 50 villages, volunteer training and a shared dataset for municipal planners.

Can we schedule a 30‑min call to discuss timelines and municipal coordination?

Best regards,
Marko Petrović
Senior GIS Analyst & Cartographer
marko.petrovic@example.org

persona.name: Marko Petrović

persona.profession: Senior GIS Analyst & Cartographer — Village-scale mapping and spatial data analyst
persona.education: MSc in Geomatics (University of Belgrade); BSc in Geography; Esri ArcGIS Professional Certification; Certified QGIS trainer; UAV/drone mapping course
persona.brief_background: Marko blends time in the field with long evenings at his workstation, stitching together satellite imagery, drone captures and interviews with elders to produce detailed village maps. He looks for patterns in settlement changes and infrastructure gaps so NGOs and municipal planners can make practical decisions.
persona.interests_lifestyle: drone piloting and aerial photography, OpenStreetMap contributions, hiking and field surveys in rural areas, Balkan folk music and village festivals, Python and R scripting for spatial analysis, map design and cartographic aesthetics, weekend camping with a field GPS, mentoring university students

general_writing_style.tone: Professional and pragmatic with a quietly warm, mentoring undercurrent. Prefers clear, actionable communication — answers questions directly, flags uncertainties, and defers to local knowledge when relevant. Slightly informal with colleagues and volunteers, more formal with institutional partners or written deliverables.
general_writing_style.syntax: Predominantly short to medium-length declarative and imperative sentences for instructions and reports, with occasional longer complex sentences when explaining methodology or interpreting spatial patterns. Often structures technical notes as stepwise numbered instructions or compact paragraphs with parenthetical clarifications (e.g., coordinates, CRS codes). Rarely uses ornate language; prioritizes clarity and reproducibility.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Mixes GIS and cartographic terminology with local place-language; routinely uses terms like "DEM", "orthorectify", "NDVI", "shapefile", "raster/vector", "GPX" and CRS tags such as "EPSG:4326". Uses metric units (meters, hectares, kilometres) and local toponyms with diacritics (e.g., "selo", "Niš", "Belgrade") when referring to field sites. Prefers domain-specific verbs like "georeference", "reproject", "tile", "clip", "attribute" and practical phrases such as "field survey" and "push edits to OSM."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequently opens notes with pragmatic markers like "Quick note:", "FYI," or "Tip:" and closes offers to help with "If you want, I can…" or "Let me know and I’ll…". Uses contractions in informal exchanges ("I'll", "can't", "we've") and includes inline technical reminders such as "check projection", "reproject to EPSG:3857" or "push to OSM"; also habitually appends coordinates or examples in parentheses, e.g., "(43.3155 N, 21.8958 E)".

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: Email to an elder or local contact arranging a respectful field interview and offering time options.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Respectful, warm, and clear with a gentle tone; use short sentences and deference to their schedule. Include practical notes (meeting place, approximate duration) parenthetically and offer flexibility and compensation details succinctly.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Polite openers: "Greetings," or "Dear [Name]," and accommodating phrases: "Whenever it suits you", "about 30–45 minutes". Include simple logistical phrases: "meet at the school (centre of selo)", "I will bring a printed map" and closers like "Thank you — I appreciate your time."

task_instruction: Ask an elder for a morning or afternoon field interview at the village school.
task_details: Write a respectful email to an elder named Milena in selo Gornji Prnjavor asking for a field interview to discuss local paths and infrastructure. Offer two time windows (morning or afternoon) on a specific date, state estimated duration (about 30–45 minutes), note meeting place as the school (centre of selo), mention you will bring a printed map and a small stipend (1,500 RSD) for their time, and offer flexibility if another time suits them. Close with a polite thanks.
personalized:
Dear Milena,

Greetings. I hope you are well. I am working on a village map for Gornji Prnjavor and would very much like to speak with you about the old footpaths and the main water points. The interview should take about 30–45 minutes. Would you be available on Tuesday 10 March in the morning (around 09:00) or in the afternoon (around 15:00)? I can meet you at the school (centre of selo). I will bring a printed map to mark places together (and my GPS if you want coordinates). I can offer a small stipend of 1,500 RSD for your time, or we can arrange transport reimbursement if that helps.

Whenever it suits you, let me know which time is best or suggest another day. If you prefer, I can come to your home instead.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
Senior GIS Analyst
(If you want, I can send a short summary after the visit.)

task_instruction: Invite an elder to a late afternoon interview with photo consent and a printed map.
task_details: Email elder named Stanko from selo Mala Reka offering a late afternoon interview on two possible days. State duration about 30–45 minutes, meeting place at the small kafana near the bridge, note you'll take a few photos for map reference and ask for consent, state compensation (coffee and 1,000 RSD), and offer a phone call to arrange alternative times.
personalized:
Dear Stanko,

Greetings. I hope this message finds you well. I am updating the map of Mala Reka and would like to ask you about seasonal crossings and where the road gets damaged in winter. The visit will take about 30–45 minutes. Could we meet late afternoon on Thursday 12 March or Friday 13 March around 17:00 at the kafana by the bridge (near the old oak)? I will bring a printed map and a notebook.

I would like to take a few simple photos to mark locations on the map; please let me know if that is alright with you. I will also bring coffee and a small thank-you of 1,000 RSD. If those times don’t work, we can arrange by phone any time that suits you.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If useful, I can mark GPS points while we walk.)

task_instruction: Request an interview at the elder's home with flexible timing and transport offered.
task_details: Write to elder named Jela in selo Donji Vinogradi offering to visit her home at any convenient time (weekdays or weekend). Specify estimated duration (about 30–45 minutes), say you'll bring a printed map and GPS device, offer to pick her up or cover transport costs (2,500 RSD), and explain the purpose: village infrastructure mapping for municipal planning. Close politely.
personalized:
Dear Jela,

Greetings. I am mapping key infrastructure in Donji Vinogradi for a small municipal planning project and would greatly value your local knowledge. The conversation would take about 30–45 minutes. I can come to your home whenever it suits you, weekdays or the weekend.

I will bring a printed map and a GPS device to check locations together. If it is easier, I can pick you up or cover transport (2,500 RSD). Please tell me a day and time that are best for you.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
Senior GIS Analyst
(If you prefer, we can do a short phone call first.)

task_instruction: Arrange an early-morning interview at the churchyard with mention of recording and summary report.
task_details: Email elder named Nikola in selo Brdo requesting an early-morning meeting at the churchyard to talk about historical settlement shifts. Mention duration about 30–45 minutes, that you would like to make a short audio recording for accuracy (ask permission), that you will bring a printed map, and that you will send a simple summary after the visit. Offer a small honorarium (2,000 RSD) and flexibility to meet another time.
personalized:
Dear Nikola,

Greetings. I hope you are well. I am preparing a short map and note on how Brdo has changed over the decades and would be grateful for your recollections. Can we meet early morning at the churchyard (around 08:30) on Saturday 14 March? The meeting will take about 30–45 minutes.

For accuracy, may I make a short audio recording of our conversation? I will only use it to check place names and then delete it. I will bring a printed map and later send you a simple summary of what we note. I can offer 2,000 RSD for your time. If that morning is not good, please tell me another time that suits you.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you prefer, we will not record — just say so.)

task_instruction: Propose a weekend interview at the market with a printed map and option to include a neighbour.
task_details: Write to elder named Radojka in selo Kamenica suggesting a short meeting at the Saturday market to discuss shared water sources and access routes. Mention duration (about 30–45 minutes), meeting place at the market stall near the fountain, that you'll bring a printed map, compensation (1,500 RSD) and invite them to bring a neighbour if they'd like. Offer alternate weekday times.
personalized:
Dear Radojka,

Greetings. I am working on mapping water sources and access routes for Kamenica and would like to ask your advice. Could we meet at the Saturday market by the fountain (near your usual stall) on 15 March for about 30–45 minutes? I will bring a printed map.

You are welcome to bring a neighbour if you think they can add details. I will offer 1,500 RSD for your time. If the market is not convenient, I can meet on a weekday at your preferred time.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you want, I can send a quick text to confirm.)

task_instruction: Invite an elder to an interview focused on seasonal road problems with an afternoon option and GPS checks.
task_details: Email elder named Ilija in selo Kruška asking to meet in the afternoon to discuss seasonal road closures and where to place emergency signs. State duration (about 30–45 minutes), meeting place at the crossroads near the bus stop, say you'll bring a printed map and will check GPS coordinates (EPSG:4326), offer transport reimbursement (1,800 RSD), and offer to change time if needed.
personalized:
Dear Ilija,

Greetings. I hope you are well. I am mapping places in Kruška that cause trouble in heavy rain and would like your input on where to place warning signs. The meeting will take about 30–45 minutes. Can we meet this Wednesday afternoon at 16:00 at the crossroads by the bus stop? I will bring a printed map and a GPS (coordinates in EPSG:4326) so we can mark exact spots.

I can cover transport costs of 1,800 RSD. If that time is not convenient, please tell me when is better.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you want, I can push the data to OSM and show you later.)

Prefers clear, actionable communication — answers questions directly, flags uncertainties, and defers to local knowledge when relevant. general_writing_style.syntax: Predominantly short to medium-length declarative and imperative sentences for instructions and reports, with occasional longer complex sentences when explaining methodology or interpreting spatial patterns. Often structures technical notes as stepwise numbered instructions or compact paragraphs with parenthetical clarifications (e.g., coordinates, CRS codes). Rarely uses ornate language; prioritizes clarity and reproducibility.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Mixes GIS and cartographic terminology with local place-language; routinely uses terms like "DEM", "orthorectify", "NDVI", "shapefile", "raster/vector", "GPX" and CRS tags such as "EPSG:4326". Uses metric units (meters, hectares, kilometres) and local toponyms with diacritics (e.g., "selo", "Niš", "Belgrade") when referring to field sites. general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequently opens notes with pragmatic markers like "Quick note:", "FYI," or "Tip:" and closes offers to help with "If you want, I can…" or "Let me know and I’ll…". Uses contractions in informal exchanges ("I'll", "can't", "we've") and includes inline technical reminders such as "check projection", "reproject to EPSG:3857" or "push to OSM"; also habitually appends coordinates or examples in parentheses, e.g., "(43.3155 N, 21.8958 E)".

task_instruction: Request permission for drone overflight discussion and schedule options.
task_details: Write to elder named Bojana in selo Vrdnik to request a meeting to discuss a planned drone flight for aerial photos near the fields. Offer two days/times (morning or late afternoon), state meeting place at the village council office, estimated duration (about 30–45 minutes), say you'll bring a printed map and explain you will not fly over private houses without consent. Offer a small reimbursement (2,500 RSD).
personalized:
Dear Bojana,

Greetings. I hope you are well. I am planning a short drone survey over the village outskirts to update field boundaries and would like your permission and local advice. Could we meet at the village council office (centre of selo) either on Monday morning at 09:00 or Tuesday late afternoon at 17:30? The meeting will take about 30–45 minutes.

I will bring a printed map and will not fly over private houses without explicit permission. I can offer 2,500 RSD for your time. If neither time suits you, tell me when is best and I will come then.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you want, I can show sample photos from previous flights.)

task_instruction: Arrange a field walk interview to validate footpath locations and offer a morning or afternoon choice.
task_details: Email elder named Stana in selo Petrovo requesting a short field walk to validate footpaths (about 30–45 minutes walking, meet at the school). Offer either morning or afternoon on a specific date, promise to bring printed map and GPS, mention small stipend (1,200 RSD), and offer to include her family member if helpful.
personalized:
Dear Stana,

Greetings. I am updating paths on the map of Petrovo and would like to confirm a few routes on foot. Could we meet at the school (centre of selo) on Sunday 22 March for a short walk of about 30–45 minutes? I can do morning or afternoon — whichever suits you.

I will bring a printed map and a GPS. I can offer 1,200 RSD for your time and you are welcome to bring a family member to help. If Sunday does not suit, please tell me another day.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you want, I can add the new paths to OSM and show you.)

task_instruction: Invite elder to a midday interview about water springs with an offer to bring printed map and tea.
task_details: Write to elder named Dragutin in selo Toplica proposing a midday meeting to discuss the location and condition of natural springs. Give estimated duration (about 30–45 minutes), meeting place at the mayor's office, state you'll bring a printed map and offer to bring tea and a small honorarium (1,000 RSD). Provide flexibility for other times.
personalized:
Dear Dragutin,

Greetings. I am mapping natural springs and their condition in Toplica and would value your knowledge. Could we meet midday (around 12:30) at the mayor's office on Thursday 26 March? The meeting will take about 30–45 minutes.

I will bring a printed map and, if you like, I can bring tea. I will also offer a small honorarium of 1,000 RSD. If another time is easier for you, just tell me when.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you want, I can record our agreed locations with GPS.)

task_instruction: Ask an elder for permission to record oral history during the visit and give evening meeting options.
task_details: Email elder named Milorad in selo Javor to request an evening interview about historical land use and terraces. State meeting place at his house or the square, estimated duration (about 30–45 minutes), mention you would like to record the conversation for accuracy and ask for consent, offer 2,000 RSD, and allow alternative times.
personalized:
Dear Milorad,

Greetings. I hope you are well. I am documenting historical land use and terracing in Javor and would appreciate your memories. Could we meet in the evening (around 19:00) at your house or at the village square on Friday 27 March? The talk would take about 30–45 minutes.

I would like to make a short audio recording to ensure I spell place names correctly; please tell me if that is not okay. I can offer 2,000 RSD for your time. If the evening is inconvenient, we can schedule another time.

Thank you — I appreciate your time.

Marko Petrović
(If you want, I will send you the recording and delete it on request.)
